Subject: Closing the reminder tool, and thank you

Dear Ms Kulkarni,

Pankaj and I ran the tests you suggested for six weeks. We called ninety clinics and got a few polite demos, and not one asked to pay. We sat with that on Sunday and agreed to close, so I wanted you to hear it from me first.

On Monday we refunded every advance payment, all fourteen of them. Today we send our users a thank-you note. Our codebase notes, with what we tried and what failed, go into a shared folder that anyone can read.

I am sad, honestly, but there is relief too, and mostly gratitude for the time you gave us. We hope to ask for your advice again on whatever comes next.

Warm regards,
Gautam

qa.q: How many advance payments did Gautam and Pankaj refund?
qa.a: They refunded all fourteen advance payments.

qa.q: How does Gautam feel about closing the company?
qa.a: Gautam feels sad but also relieved and grateful, saying so plainly in the closing lines.

qa.q: What other approach could the founders have tried before closing, and why?
qa.a: They could have interviewed the clinics that said no to find the root cause, which might have shown a fixable problem, though six weeks of tests already gave a clear answer.

qa.q: How might the users who paid in advance see the way the company closed?
qa.a: They get their money back and a thank-you, so they are more likely to trust Gautam and Pankaj on a future venture. 🙂

grounding: The email shows founders ending the product after tests show no demand, refunding customers, thanking users and sharing notes.

Hrithik, you asked what I'm proudest of from my first company. Not the product. The ending. I'm Rekha, and two years ago my co-founder and I ran six weeks of tests on our home-tutor booking idea. Clear targets. We missed every one: almost no repeat bookings, and parents told us plainly they'd stick with the tutor next door.
So we stopped. We refunded every parent who had paid in advance, all thirty-one of them, within ten days. We wrote each of our two hundred users a real thank-you note, not a form email. And we put our code notes and what we'd learned into a document for any founder who asked.
It hurt. But last month, when I pitched my new company, one investor said, "You're the ones who refunded everyone." That's why she took the meeting, Hrithik.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel about stopping, then and now?
qa.a: Stopping hurt Rekha at the time, but now Rekha feels proud of how cleanly they ended it.

qa.q: Which part of the shutdown helped Rekha most later, and why?
qa.a: Refunding everyone quickly, because it built a reputation that made an investor take the next meeting.

qa.q: How might the parents who got refunds see Rekha's team?
qa.a: They would likely feel respected and trust the team, since they got their money back quickly and honestly.

grounding: It shows founders ending a startup after six weeks of failed tests by refunding advance payments, thanking users and sharing code notes, which protects their reputation.

I was the first engineer Deepika hired, so I was in the room when she decided. For six weeks she had tested whether offices would pay for healthy lunch subscriptions. The target was fifty paying offices. We reached nine.
She didn't hide it. On a Monday she put the number on the screen and said, "We're winding down. Properly." That week I watched her personally call every customer who had paid in advance and arrange refunds. She wrote to each of our users to thank them. She asked me to tidy our code notes into a shared folder with a readme, "so someone can learn from what we built".
I don't know how she felt at night. In the office she was steady. On the last day she took us to lunch and handed each of us a reference letter, already written.
— Arnab

qa.q: How many paying offices did they reach?
qa.a: Nine, against a target of fifty.

qa.q: What might Deepika have been feeling during the wind-down?
qa.a: She may have felt sad and disappointed, though in the office she stayed steady; Arnab can't know how she felt at night.

qa.q: What else could Deepika do to keep good relationships after closing?
qa.a: Stay in touch with customers and the team, and share what the tests taught her with other founders who ask.

qa.q: How does Arnab experience the way the company closed?
qa.a: Arnab sees it as honest and caring: refunds, thank-you notes, tidy code notes and a ready reference letter.

grounding: It shows a founder deciding to wind down after six weeks of tests show no demand, refunding advances, thanking users and sharing code notes.
